article.scope: Generic tiltmeter class: an instrument whose main measurement is the tilt (inclination) of the ground or an instrument platform relative to the local gravity direction, including tidal and thermal tilt. Seismometers (payloads 001 to 004) and geophones (005) are tilt-sensitive; their tilt or tidal outputs are described here only where used as a science channel, and their seismic function is covered in 001 to 004. Strainmeters (019) and tidal deformation sensors (025) measure related deformation; gravimeters (016) measure gravity. Lunar libration is payload 024.
article.overview: A tiltmeter reports how far the ground, or an instrument platform, is inclined from level. On the Moon, tilt changes come mainly from Earth-raised tides, from heating and cooling of the surface and of equipment, and from slow crustal deformation. No dedicated flown lunar tiltmeter was identified in the sources read. The main flown lunar tilt record comes from the Apollo 12 Passive Seismic Experiment (PSE), whose horizontal seismometers were tilt-sensitive, were leveled by a gimbal, and produced a separate tidal output. The Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report states that the PSE was capable of measuring tilts of the lunar surface and changes in gravity at the instrument location [1]. Two entries are non-flown reference points: a tilt-sensor concept in the Lunar Gravitational-wave Antenna (LGWA) mission study [4], and a terrestrial mechanical tiltmeter reported in 2014 [3].
article.description: Tilt is an angle, expressed in radians or in microradians (µrad) and nanoradians (nrad). The Apollo 12 PSR reports large tilts of 0.5 to 1 minute of arc at the PSE site during terminator passage [1]. One minute of arc is about 2.9 × 10⁻⁴ radians, so the reported range corresponds to roughly 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ to 2.9 × 10⁻⁴ radians (this is a unit conversion of the PSR value, not a separate measurement). A tiltmeter differs from a level in that it converts a small angular change into a continuously recorded signal with a time reference. Sensing elements include pendulums, suspended proof masses, beam balances, liquid or bubble sensors, and the horizontal channel of a seismometer. Lunar tilt measurements serve two purposes: science (tidal and slow thermal or tectonic tilt) and correction. The LGWA study notes that a tilt sensor could allow ground-tilt noise to be subtracted from a horizontal displacement measurement [4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a lunar tiltmeter is to measure slow, direction-dependent changes in the surface. The Apollo 12 PSE was designed to detect surface vibrations and to measure tilts and gravity changes at its site [1]. Tidal tilt was a stated target. The PSR describes the horizontal long-period seismometers as tilt-sensitive and the vertical long-period seismometer as sensitive to changes in gravity, with the two outputs recorded on separate feedback or tidal channels [1]. Tilt measurements also support engineering. The LGWA study states that its platform must be held level to within 10 µrad, that initial leveling will be needed to compensate ground slope, and that regular or perhaps continuous adjustment may be needed because ground tilts vary with time [4]. Tilt records would therefore help plan the operation of a long-lived station.
article.operating_principle: A sensor that tries to stay aligned with gravity appears to move when its platform tilts. For a small tilt θ in radians, a horizontal sensor axis sees a change in the gravity component along it of about g × θ, where g is local surface gravity. A horizontal seismometer therefore responds to both tilt and ground motion, and separating them needs a second sensor, a known tilt reference, or a response model. This is why tilt-sensitive seismometers need careful leveling. The Apollo 12 PSE horizontal long-period seismometers are described as very sensitive to tilt and must be leveled to high accuracy [1]. The instrument was leveled by a two-axis motor-driven gimbal, with a third motor adjusting the vertical long-period seismometer. Motors were controlled by ground command through 15 commands governing leveling direction and speed, instrument gain and calibration [1]. The PSR states that the feedback or tidal output carries the slow tilt information [1]. A 2014 terrestrial design reports a built rotation sensor and a tiltmeter with sensitivity better than 1 nrad/√Hz above 30 mHz [3]. This is a ground instrument, and no lunar application is discussed.
article.scientific_importance: Tilt records add a direct measure of the surface response to tides and temperature. The Apollo 12 PSR reports that large tilts occur at terminator crossings and that they most likely result from thermal effects, with rapid heating and cooling of the Mylar thermal shroud a major source [1]. Tilt mistaken for ground motion can produce false seismic signals, so tilt identification matters for seismic interpretation. The PSR also states that the expected temperature range at the PSE site, from +85 °F (predicted by extrapolation) during the lunar night to +142 °F during the lunar day, would not degrade seismic data but will greatly reduce the probability of obtaining useful tidal data [1]. Thermal disturbance can therefore obscure the slow tidal signal that a tiltmeter most wants to measure.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, range, power or sensitivity for a tiltmeter. The examples use different sensing principles and status levels and are not comparable, so no comparison table is given. Values are tied to each named instrument and source. Where a value is not stated in the source read, the entry says so.

examples.name: Apollo 12 Passive Seismic Experiment, tilt-sensitive horizontal seismometers
examples.type: Flown lunar surface instrument (tilt as a by-product of a seismometer)
examples.status: Flown on the Moon. The PSR reports the PSE operated successfully throughout the first 42 days of the experiment, the period covered by the report [1].
examples.mass_note: The sensor is constructed principally of beryllium and weighs 11.5 kg, including the electronics module and thermal insulation [1]. The same figure is used in the PSE article (payload 001).
examples.sensor_configuration: Three matched long-period seismometers aligned orthogonally (one vertical, two horizontal), plus a single-axis short-period seismometer for vertical motion [1].
examples.leveling: The horizontal sensors are leveled by a two-axis motor-driven gimbal. A third motor adjusts the vertical long-period seismometer. The PSR figure schematic labels a gnomon (Sun compass) and a level sensor on the thermal shroud [1]. No leveling accuracy for the PSE is stated in the section read.
examples.tilt_and_gravity_outputs: Feedback or tidal outputs: horizontal long-period outputs respond to tilt; vertical long-period output responds to changes in gravity [1]. No calibrated tilt sensitivity in radians is stated in the section read.
examples.observed_tilts: Large tilts of 0.5 to 1 minute of arc during terminator passage over the PSE site, when thermal changes were most rapid. Tilting began several hours before a day-to-night crossing and lasted several days; tilting began abruptly at a night-to-day crossing and lasted several days [1].
examples.thermal_control: Aluminised Mylar thermal shroud and a 2.5 W heater with a proportional controller [1]. Higher-than-anticipated heater output was required to keep the sensor unit within its temperature tolerance [1].
examples.caging_and_uncaging: A caging system secured critical elements during transport and deployment using pressurised bellows; uncaging was performed on command by piercing the connecting line with a small explosive device [1].
examples.calibration: A known current step is applied to each seismometer coil by ground command, equivalent to a known step of ground acceleration [1].
examples.power_dimensions: Not stated in the PSR section read.
examples.qualification: Flown instrument. Tilt performance is described qualitatively in the PSR; no calibrated tilt-sensitivity figure in radians is given.

examples.name: Lunar Gravitational-wave Antenna (LGWA) platform tilt concept
examples.status: Proposed mission study for an array of advanced inertial sensors to monitor the Moon's response to gravitational waves. No flight hardware, prototype or mission approval is described in the sections read [4].
examples.leveling_requirement_note: The study states that the horizontal alignment of the LIGS platform must be accurate to within 10 µrad (Section 2.1.1). This is a design requirement, not a measured performance [4].
examples.tilt_measurement_option: The study describes a sensor deployed with the ability to measure ground tilts in addition to ground displacement, citing another source, and notes that the tilt measurement could be used to subtract tilt-induced noise from the displacement measurement [4]. No specification for that sensor is given.
examples.tidal_tilt_reported_by_secondary_summary: A secondary search summary gives a peak tidal tilt of about 5 × 10⁻⁶ rad. Not verified in the sections read; not used as a specification.
examples.power_dimensions_sensitivity: Not stated in the sections read.
examples.qualification: Proposed concept only; no flight or prototype qualification is claimed.

examples.name: Mechanical absolute-rotation sensor and tiltmeter (2014)
examples.type: Built terrestrial instrument (not flown, not lunar)
examples.status: A built device reported in a 2014 journal paper. The abstract describes it as useful for rotational seismology and for rejecting rotation signals from seismometers, for example in Advanced LIGO. No lunar application is discussed [3].

sensitivity.absolute_rotation_sensor: Less than 1 nrad/√Hz above 30 mHz and 0.2 nrad/√Hz above 100 mHz, about a single horizontal axis [3].

examples.design_detail_note: A search summary describes a meter-scale beam balance read optically with an autocollimator. This detail was not on the abstract page read and is not relied on here [3].
examples.power_dimensions: Not stated in the part of the paper read.
examples.qualification: Ground instrument. No lunar environmental qualification is described.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No single dimension set applies to a tiltmeter class. The flown Apollo 12 PSE's dimensions are not stated in the PSR section read. Dimensions for the LGWA concept and the 2014 terrestrial device are not stated in the sources read.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The Apollo 12 PSE sensor is stated at 11.5 kg including electronics module and thermal insulation [1]. Mass for the LGWA concept and the 2014 terrestrial device is not stated in the sources read.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Apollo 12 PSE thermal system used a 2.5 W heater, and the PSR reports that higher-than-anticipated heater output was required [1]. Total PSE power is not stated in the section read. Power for the LGWA concept and the 2014 terrestrial device is not stated in the sources read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar tiltmeter must cope with a large temperature cycle and with the thermal gradients that drive tilt. The Apollo 12 PSR shows that tilt at the PSE site was driven by thermal changes at terminator crossings rather than by seismic activity [1]. Thermal insulation, shielding and temperature control are therefore part of the tilt measurement, not only survival design, and the PSR reports that more heater output than anticipated was needed [1]. The surface must be stable and must not change its slope during measurement. The LGWA study notes that initial leveling and possibly continuous adjustment may be needed where tilts vary with time [4], and that burial of stations outside permanently shadowed regions is proposed to avoid excess noise from temperature-driven tilts; no depth or tilt values are given [4]. Commanding is an operational requirement: the Apollo 12 PSE needed ground commands for leveling motors, gain and calibration [1].
article.limitations: A horizontal seismometer's output mixes ground acceleration and tilt in the same channel. The LGWA study notes that ground tilt is a source of noise for horizontal sensing [4], so a separate tilt measurement is needed to separate the two cleanly. Thermal tilt can dominate: the Apollo 12 PSR reports tilts of 0.5 to 1 minute of arc at terminator crossings, likely thermal in origin [1]. A much smaller slow tidal tilt would be hard to recover without a thermal model or thermal control. Leveling depends on commanded motors, and a single tiltmeter records tilt at one point and cannot map a tilt field over a region.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The Apollo 12 PSE was carried to the Moon and deployed by the astronauts as part of the Apollo surface experiments. Its caging system protected critical elements in transport and was released by command [1]. After deployment, leveling was performed by commanded motors [1]. Deployment method is historical and is not evidence of how a future tiltmeter would be delivered.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth.
Launch it with a launch vehicle and transfer it toward the Moon.
Land it on the surface with the lander.
Release or deploy the sensor, using a caging or restraint system to protect it in transport (as the Apollo 12 PSE did [1]).
Level the sensor, by commanded motors or by an equivalent method, and connect power, thermal and communications interfaces.
Verify tilt, temperature and data behaviour after deployment.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo 12 PSE: astronaut deployment, caging with pressurised bellows, uncaging by command with a small explosive device, and gimbal leveling by ground command [1]. No stowage position on the lunar module is described in the section read. Future deployment methods are not described in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 12 PSE is the flown example of a tilt-sensitive instrument on the Moon [1]. The LGWA study is a proposed example of platform leveling and tilt-noise subtraction [4]. The 2014 device is a terrestrial example [3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: This article does not assert compatibility with any named lander, rover or spacecraft. Compatibility would need to be assessed from mass, dimensions, mounting interface, leveling method, thermal requirements, power, commanding and deployment method. None of these were verified for a named lander in the sources read. No lunar landing-site recommendation is included.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 12 PSE is the clearest flown example of a lunar instrument that measured tilt. Its Preliminary Science Report recorded thermally driven terminator tilts, treated them as a disturbance, and identified the tidal and feedback outputs as the channel for slow tilt information [1]. The report also recognised that the temperature environment would reduce the chance of obtaining useful tidal data [1]. The sources read do not show specific later instrument decisions that followed from these findings. Later proposals treat tilt as both a design constraint and a measurement: the LGWA mission study (2024) describes platform leveling and tilt-noise subtraction for a proposed lunar inertial sensor array [4]. The 2014 terrestrial tiltmeter shows the sensitivity reached by mechanical ground tilt sensors [3].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No flown dedicated lunar tiltmeter was identified in the sources read, so the flown lunar record is a seismometer's tilt output. The PSR does not give a calibrated tilt sensitivity in radians for the PSE. The PSE dimensions and operating power are not in the section read. The LGWA 10 µrad requirement is a design requirement. The LGWA tidal-tilt figure and the 2014 beam-balance detail come from secondary summaries and are not used as specifications.

data_quality_notes: Scope: generic tiltmeter class (tilt/inclination of ground or platform relative to gravity). Seismometers (001 to 004), geophones (005), strainmeters (019), tidal deformation sensors (025), gravimeters (016) and libration (024) are cross-referenced, not repeated.

No flown dedicated lunar tiltmeter was identified in the sources read. The flown lunar tilt record is the Apollo 12 PSE horizontal seismometers' tilt and tidal output. A searched lunar tiltmeter proposal was not found; this does not establish that none exists.

Apollo 12 PSR Section 3 was read from its full text layer (pdftotext) at the WUSTL PDF URL. Tilt statements (0.5 to 1 arcmin, terminator and thermal behaviour, gimbal leveling, 15 commands, tidal and feedback outputs, caging, calibration, 2.5 W heater, 11.5 kg mass) are primary-source statements.
Apollo 12 PSE dimensions, operating power and a calibrated tilt sensitivity in radians are not stated in the PSR section read. They are recorded as not stated.
Conversion of 0.5 to 1 arcminute to radians (approximately 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ to 2.9 × 10⁻⁴ rad) is an arithmetic conversion made for this article, not a published measurement.

Apollo 14 PSE gnomon and level sensor, and an intermittent gimbal-motor fault on Apollo 14, come from a secondary summary. They are not verified against the Apollo 14 primary report and are not used as specifications.

LGWA: the 10 µrad platform alignment requirement was read from the HTML version of arXiv:2404.09181 (Section 2.1.1). The LGWA tilt-sensor concept cites another source (Li et al.), which was not read; no tilt sensor specifications are available.

LGWA tidal tilt of about 5 × 10⁻⁶ rad and the 'few tens of microradians' leveling statement came from search summaries only. They are not verified in the sections read and are not used as specifications.
LGWA journal publication (JCAP, 2025) is from a search summary; not verified on the paper.

2014 terrestrial device (arXiv:1401.4412): sensitivity figures and the ground-instrument framing were read from the abstract page only. The beam-balance and autocollimator detail comes from a search summary and is not used. No lunar application is discussed in the abstract.
